item.title: Forecasting the Ambient Solar Wind With a Physics-Informed Learned Inner Boundary: Part I-Differentiable Inverse Reconstruction From Solar Images
item.description: arXiv:2611.01310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The solar-wind speed at the inner boundary of heliospheric models is not observed; near-Earth monitors record the wind only after nonlinear propagation. We pose the reconstruction of an effective boundary speed at $21.5\,R_\odot$ as an inverse problem and train a map from solar observations to that boundary by differentiating through a reduced heliospheric transport solver from 21.5$\,R_\odot$ to measurement locations near the L1 Lagrangian point. Screening 42 candidate features from SDO/AIA 193~\AA{} images and SDO/HMI magnetograms identifies coronal-hole area, its proximity to the ecliptic and its darkness as the most informative; the reference model adds their recent history, the expansion factor of GONG-based potential-field models and the speed observed one rotation earlier. In five-fold chronological cross-validation over solar cycle 24, the reconstruction outperforms 27-day recurrence and a linear regression on the screened features at a fixed lead (ROC area for wind above 600~km~s$^{-1}$: 0.879 versus 0.802 and 0.850) with a predicted-to-observed standard-deviation ratio of 0.81, at the cost of a $+26$~km~s$^{-1}$ bias from its tail-weighted loss. A factorial comparison shows that the skill comes from training through a speed-dependent propagation: a fixed lag degrades the score by 8.6~km~s$^{-1}$, stream interaction adds little, and a linear map, or a model with one coefficient per physical quantity, matches the neural network. About 57\% of the variance of the hourly speed is not determined by these inputs, and the remaining error is common to all model classes: better reconstructions need more informative inputs rather than more flexible models. Forecasting and probabilistic prediction are addressed in Parts II and III.
item.dc:creator: Enrico Camporeale, Andong Hu, Prateek Mayank, Thomas E. Berger

item.title: The Neural Density Model: An Open 3D Thermospheric Density Reanalysis for 2003--2026 From Tracked Space Debris
item.description: arXiv:2611.02103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermospheric mass density controls satellite drag but is observed directly by few missions, and the leading operational product (HASDM) relies on non-public radar data. We present the Neural Density Model (NDM), a 3D density reanalysis for October 2003--October 2026 at 250--800~km. Previous approaches either convert the orbital decay of tracked objects into point densities or correct empirical models with a few global scale factors. NDM instead fits a spatially resolved neural correction to NRLMSISE-00 directly to the observed decay of 600--800 objects per year, through a differentiable drag operator, jointly with their ballistic coefficients, calibration spheres and accelerometer densities. On withheld satellites the median error is 0.078 (natural-log units), against 0.101 for HASDM and 0.310 for NRLMSISE-00; NDM has the smaller bias, HASDM slightly smaller scatter. On Spire GNSS orbits, never used in training, NDM and HASDM perform comparably. NDM uses only public observations.
item.dc:creator: Enrico Camporeale

item.title: Solving the Mystery of the Electron Radiation Belt at Uranus: Leveraging Knowledge of Earth's Radiation Belts in a Re-Examination of Voyager 2 Observations
item.description: arXiv:2611.02221v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Voyager 2 provided the only direct measurement of the radiation environment at Uranus and established the well-accepted characterization of a system with a weaker ion radiation belt and surprisingly intense electron radiation belt. Recent re-analysis of the flyby, however, suggests that these observations were not taken during normal solar wind conditions, and instead occurred while a large solar wind transient, a corotating interaction region, was passing over the system. With this context, this study compares the Voyager 2 observations to a similar event observed at Earth. This comparative approach, along with an expanded contextual interpretation of the Voyager 2 flyby, suggests that solar wind-magnetospheric interactions at Uranus may have driven enhanced lower band chorus wave emissions capable of accelerating electrons to relativistic energies. This motivates new, more expansive questions to be explored at Uranus and highlights the need for a Uranus orbiter mission.
item.dc:creator: R. C. Allen, S. K. Vines, G. C. Ho

item.title: Radial Evolution of a CIR: Observations From a Nearly Radially Aligned Event Between Parker Solar Probe and STEREO-A
item.description: arXiv:2611.02224v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The addition of Parker Solar Probe (PSP) to the Heliophysics System Observatory has allowed for the unprecedented ability to study Corotating Interaction Regions (CIRs) at multiple radial distances without significant temporal/longitudinal variations. On September 19, 2019, PSP observed a CIR at $\sim$0.5 au when it was nearly radially aligned with the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory-Ahead (STEREO-A) spacecraft at $\sim$1 au, allowing for an unambiguous assessment of the radial evolution of a single CIR. Bulk plasma and magnetic field signatures of the CIR evolve in a fashion characteristic to previous observations; however, the suprathermal ions are enhanced over a larger longitudinal range at PSP than at STEREO-A, although at much lower intensities. The longitudinal spread appears to be largely a consequence of magnetic field line topology at CIRs between the compressed slow solar wind upstream and high-speed stream following the CIR, underscoring the importance of the large-scale topology of these structures.

item.title: Structure of energy flux densities in Earth's magnetotail reconnection regions: Bridging simulation and observation
item.description: arXiv:2611.02870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magnetic reconnection is important in both space and laboratory contexts because it changes the topology of magnetic fields and converts magnetic energy into particle energies. Establishing where this energy conversion occurs is critical for understanding how reconnection partitions energy. Using a novel machine learning approach based on simulations that explicitly identifies the separatrix regions for the first time, the partition of energy flux densities within the magnetic reconnection site is evaluated through statistical study of magnetotail reconnection events observed in situ. The separatrices are found to have the largest electron energy flux densities, roughly twice those in the exhaust, and Poynting flux densities about four times those in the inflows, whereas typical ion enthalpy flux densities are largest in the exhaust. The separatrices are therefore sites of intense electron and electromagnetic energy transport, although their small thickness means that the exhaust may still carry most of the total energy flux.
item.dc:creator: Cara L. Waters, Jonathan P. Eastwood, Harry C. Lewis, Na\"is Fargette, Marit {\O}ieroset, Tai D. Phan, David L. Newman, Martin V. Goldman

item.title: A heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent test for process noise calibration of Kalman filters in multi-sensor orbit determination
item.description: arXiv:2611.03477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Process noise calibration is a central problem in sequential orbit determination. If the process noise covariance is too small the filter is overconfident, and if it is too large it is overconservative. In both cases the estimation error grows and the reported covariance stops describing it, which affects downstream products such as conjunction assessment or re-entry prediction. No widely adopted method diagnoses the calibration in multi-sensor settings, where measurements of different type and dimension must enter a single consistency metric. This work presents the Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent Dimensionless Averaged Normalised Innovation Squared (HAC-DANIS) test, which evaluates process noise calibration from the innovation sequence of the filter, without ground truth. The normalised innovation squared (NIS) of each measurement is divided by its dimension, which puts sensors of any dimension on a common scale, and the standard error of the averaged sequence is obtained with the heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent (HAC) Newey--West estimator, which accounts for the sensor-dependent variance of the sequence and for the serial correlation left by a miscalibrated filter or an imperfect dynamical model. Under mixing and moment conditions the statistic is asymptotically standard normal for a calibrated filter, and for a miscalibrated one its sign indicates the direction of the miscalibration. The autocorrelation function of the normalised sequence complements the test with a characterisation of the mistuning regime. Applied to an unscented Kalman filter processing simulated laser, telescope and radar observations of four satellites in low Earth orbit, the test rejects the eight miscalibrated process noise configurations with the sign of their miscalibration and does not reject the four calibrated with it.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Malaver, Jose M. Montilla, Rafael Vazquez

item.title: Quantum Recovery from Black-Hole Radiation Beyond the Emission Yield
item.description: arXiv:2611.01821v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A proposed resolution of the black-hole information paradox must explain which information an outside observer can recover from escaping radiation\cite{Hawking,Page,Hayden,Almheiri}. Environmental memory can return correlations to the source without delivering them to that observer\cite{ChenQi,ChenMemory}. Here we establish a sharp recovery frontier at fixed mean radiation yield for single-excitation channels and realize its qubit limit with an autonomous quantum-memory emitter. Unequal transmissions balance retained coherence against information in failed collection events. A reference--radiation correlation test distinguishes this gain even when the mean collected energy is unchanged. Identical transmission channels instead give the same recovery at matched collection, regardless of their emission timescales. For a broader class of interacting sources, an ordering of collected and inaccessible coupling spectra forbids unassisted quantum transmission irrespective of internal memory. A separate coding example supports a positive rate where uniform transmission at matched actual yield has zero capacity. Together, these results identify what openness must change to assist recovery: the accessible transmission structure. They supply a physically constrained comparison of evaporation mechanisms, separating information delivered to radiation from coherence retained elsewhere or an increase in the collected output.
item.dc:creator: Kashif Ammar Yasir

item.title: Current Sheets and Magnetic Reconnection statistics by Solar Orbiter at few to tens of Ion Inertial Lengths II: Conditions for Reconnection, and Current Sheet Planarity
item.description: arXiv:2611.02199v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a statistical study of magnetic reconnection and current sheet (CS) properties at scales from the ion inertial length ($\delta_i$), up to 86.4 $\delta_i$. We analyze 103 hours of high-cadence (4 samples/s) in-situ Solar Orbiter ion data, collected from July 2020 to September 2022, which correspond mainly to slow and Alfv\'enic solar wind. We applied an automatic detection algorithm to find CSs of thicknesses near and above the ion inertial length ($\delta_i$), and classify them as Alfv\'enic or reconnecting. The orientation of the CSs is consistent with an isotropic distribution of the discontinuities. The median ratio of reconnection jet velocity to theoretical outflow velocity is 0.71. We find that the diamagnetic drift reconnection suppression mechanism has no impact on the cataloged CSs, due to the symmetry of their upstream conditions. We find that a flow shear in the reconnection direction suppresses magnetic reconnection, and it is consistently greater for Alfv\'enic than for reconnecting CSs. Flow shear in the guide-field direction is too small to suppress magnetic reconnection in ion scale solar wind CSs.

item.title: Comparison of models for dynamical structures of solar plasma
item.description: arXiv:2611.02818v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Possible mechanisms of generation of dynamical plasma structures are associated with the Schwarzschild criterion for convective instability and with excess energy (heat, magnetic): due to the superadiabatic temperature gradient, the overheated plasma starts to rise. In the framework of Navier-Stokes MHD equations, the complete system of equations for the full axisymmetric plasma model includes equations for the stream function, the azimuthal velocity component, the density change, the flow function of poloidal magnetic field, and the azimuthal component of the magnetic field. Within the framework of ideal hydrodynamics, the simplest plasma model is applicable to the initial stage of generation of plasma structures. In this case, rigorous analytical solutions are constructed from blocks. Within the framework of ideal hydrodynamics, some intermediate model - the refined model considers rotating plasma at the growth stage. In this case, some unidirectional differential rotation occurs. The full model studies the development of structures as rotating plasma from the very beginning to the highest development stage. The velocity field is adjusted to boundary conditions. Velocity components change in a coordinated manner. The stationary axisymmetric ambient magnetic field and its gradients have little effect on the plasma structure and velocity field. The movement structures for all models are similar. Radial flows converge towards the axis at the bottom, and there is an outflow to the periphery near the top of the plasma structure. The maximum vertical velocity component is reached at the center of the axis. Applications of these models to solar structures, including jets, are discussed.
item.dc:creator: S. N. Artekha

item.title: Solar Wind Turbulence Spectra and Correlation Scale from 4 to 50 $r_\odot$: STEREO and PUNCH Observations
item.description: arXiv:2611.03328v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the radial evolution of solar wind turbulence using remote-sensing brightness observations from the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO) and the first science-ready images from the Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) mission. Exploiting the combined wide fields of view of STEREO's COR2 coronagraph (4-9 r_sun) and PUNCH's Wide Field Imager (WFI, 21-50 r_sun), we track the radial evolution of the power spectral density and correlation scale of density fluctuations from 4 to 50 r_sun. Line-of-sight integration systematically steepens the "usual" turbulence scaling laws by a constant offset of about -0.5 across all resolved scales, so that the energy-containing range (nominally k^-1) and the inertial range (nominally k^-5/3) appear as k^-1.5 and k^-2.1, respectively -- consistent with previous synthetic-image simulations. The correlation scale increases with heliocentric distance across the full range of heliodistances probed, in accordance with previous theoretical models and observations at closer distances from the Sun.

item.title: The Equations of Reduced Magnetohydrodynamics in Dipole Coordinates
item.description: arXiv:2608.06617v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The equations of reduced magnetohydrodynamics (RMHD) isolate the Alfv\'enic energy transfer and turbulence dynamics from MHD in a computationally tractable way. In this study, we derive the equations of RMHD for a low $\beta$ plasma in a dipole coordinate system aligned with an inhomogeneous background that is general enough to represent the Earth's magnetosphere using a multiscale analysis and the Kreiss theorem. The most important effect beyond homogeneous RMHD is the propensity for background Alfv\'en speed gradients to drive nonlinear wave effects. This work has immediate application to the magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling problem in the Earth's magnetosphere, where the Alfv\'en speed varies by an order of magnitude over a short distance. We estimate the turbulent energy transfer driven by this. In Earth's magneotsphere, a substantial portion of energy ($>20\%$) could be transferred in this way along auroral field lines. A revised field aligned current density mapping technique to account for this energy loss mechanism is proposed to replace using $j_\parallel/B_0$ being constant along the field line. We also predict the existence of a ``saturation current density,'' where there is a maximum $j_\parallel$ that exist before driving a nonlinear cascade. At Earth, this value is $\sim 5\; \mu \text{A}/\text{m}^2$ at the ionosphere, which corresponds to the maximum observed value by ground magnetometers. Furthermore, this study makes use of a novel methodology, a computer algebra system, in performing algebraic work under complicated coordinate systems. We hope this approach serves as a template for performing reproducible and verifiable multiscale perturbation analysis under arbitrarily complex geometries.
item.dc:creator: Ian M. DesJardin, Christopher Bard, Natalia Y. Buzulukova, John C. Dorelli

item.title: Feasibility of Capillary-Driven Orbital Liquid Mirror Telescopes
item.description: arXiv:2608.31042v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Space-based liquid mirror telescopes (LMTs) have been recently proposed to overcome the scaling limits of traditional rigid mirrors. In these new space architectures, capillary forces would shape a reflective liquid into a spherical optical surface in microgravity. However, the equilibrium, stability, and dynamic behavior of such liquid interfaces remain largely uncharacterized under orbital perturbations. This study investigates the feasibility of space LMTs by combining axisymmetric capillary with thin-film models. Solar radiation pressure and self-gravitation are found to be the dominant perturbations in Sun--Earth L2 orbits, causing equilibrium deformations that exceed the $\lambda/20$ optical threshold at apertures above 0.86~m for visible ($\lambda = 380$~nm) and 1.58~m for near-infrared observatories ($\lambda = 2.5~\mu \mathrm{m}$). Micrometeoroid impacts self-heal within seconds to minutes, settling after filling requires years to decades at large apertures, and propulsive maneuvers breach optical limits within seconds to hours. These results highlight the need for interface control in large-scale systems such as NASA's 50~m Fluidic Telescope (FLUTE). Thermocapillary actuation supports apertures of 2.3/8.0~m (VIS/NIR) at $100~\mu \mathrm{K}$ and 10.6/37.7~m at $10~\mu \mathrm{K}$ resolution. Simultaneously, parasitic Marangoni flows impose sub-mK uniformity requirements for NIR and 1--$100~\mu \mathrm{K}$ for visible operation on any capillary LMT. Departing the capillary regime by imposing a surface-normal settling acceleration, ranging from 39~mm\,s$^{-2}$ (NIR,5~m) to 17~m\,s$^{-2}$ (VIS,50~m), is the most promising route to tens of meters in aperture. This approach enables a passive implementation, effectively suppressing perturbation induced interface distortions and thermal Marangoni flows. Keywords: Liquid mirror telescope, Optics, Space
item.dc:creator: Janoah Dietrich, \'Alvaro Romero-Calvo
